lines.text:
My Grandmother's Garden

Every spring, my grandmother spends her mornings in the garden behind her house. She grows flowers, vegetables, and herbs, and she takes care of everything herself.

The garden has a small lawn surrounded by a low hedge. Along the fence, there are flower beds full of roses, tulips, and sunflowers. She waters them every morning with a hose or a watering can, depending on how much rain there has been. If the soil is too dry, she uses a sprinkler.

In the vegetable patch, she plants tomatoes, carrots, lettuce, and peppers. She prepares the soil with a rake and a shovel before planting the seeds. Once the seedlings start to grow, she adds fertiliser and removes any weeds by hand or with a small trowel.

There is a greenhouse at the back of the garden where she grows herbs like basil and mint all year round. Inside, she keeps pots on wooden shelves and uses a thermometer to check the temperature.

She also has a compost bin where she puts leftover food and garden waste. After a few months, it turns into rich compost that she mixes into the soil.

My grandmother says that gardening keeps her active and calm. I enjoy helping her — especially when it is time to pick the ripe vegetables and bring them to the kitchen.

lines.text: In British English, 'garden' means the outdoor space around a house (front garden, back garden). In American English, 'yard' is more common for the grass area, while 'garden' means a planted area with flowers or vegetables.
lines.name: In British English, 'garden' means the outdoor space around a house (front garden, back garden). In American English, 'yard' is more common for the grass area, while 'garden' means a planted area with flowers or vegetables.

lines.text: In Britain, 'allotments' are small plots of land rented by people to grow food. They are very popular and often have long waiting lists. This concept is less common in North America.
lines.name: In Britain, 'allotments' are small plots of land rented by people to grow food. They are very popular and often have long waiting lists. This concept is less common in North America.

lines.text: A 'garden centre' sells plants, tools, pots, and garden furniture. A 'nursery' specifically grows and sells young plants and seedlings. Both terms are widely used.
